title: Streamlined Onramp: retries, idempotency & realtime params - vendor kickoff
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a hosted API onramp demo focused on realtime streaming behavior, retry/backoff strategies, and idempotency tokens. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a payments support chatbot; main concerns: tail latency, cost under concurrency, and security/compliance for PII. Action items include sending security whitepaper, sample SDK snippet for idempotency, and a follow-up pilot proposal.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-06
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood Product), Aisha Khan (Ledgerly Lead ML Eng), Tom Wu (Platform), Nora Ellis (PM), Samir Rao (Security)
---
00:00 Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we really appreciate you taking the time. We're gonna run through a short hosted API onramp focused on realtime streaming behavior, what retry strategies look like, and how you can do idempotency so your customer-facing agent doesn't hallucinate duplicates. Quick intro from everyone?
00:15 Aisha (Ledgerly): Hi, I'm Aisha, lead ML. We're looking at adding an LLM-powered support assistant for payments disputes. Very concerned about tail latency and PII handling.
00:22 Tom (Ledgerly): Tom, infra, and I'll be the one integrating the SDK into our backend, so uptime and long lived connections matter.
00:28 Nora (Ledgerly): Nora, PM; timeline is roughly a 6–8 week pilot if things look good.
00:33 Samir (Ledgerly): Samir from security; SOC2, KMS, and audit logging are must-haves.
00:38 Diego (Redwood): Awesome, thanks. Quick agenda: 1) live demo of streaming and param effects, 2) retry and backoff strategies (we'll show code snippets), 3) idempotency & dedup patterns, 4) console monitor and Optimize suggestions for batching/caching, and 5) Q+A.
01:00 Maya: Quick product positioning note — hosted API gives you fast time-to-value and transparent token-level metrics; Dedicated gives reserved capacity for predictable tail latency but requires a procurement cadence. We'll point out tradeoffs as we go.
01:18 Diego: Alright, jumping into the console. (screen share) First we make a streaming chat call. On the left is the request payload: messages, model: rdx-lite-3b, stream:true, and params temperature 0.2, top_p 0.9.
01:35 Diego: Note the response chunks arriving — token deltas. For realtime UX you want smaller initial tokens and lower temperature to reduce variability.
01:50 Nora: Quick question: how do you recommend balancing token size vs latency for short responses?
01:55 Diego: Good question. If you expect concise answers (one or two sentences) set max_tokens low — say 40 — and use a lower temperature. Also reduce the chunk size by configuring the client-side partial flush (we have an SDK option) so the stream is emitted earlier. That lowers perceived latency.
02:20 Aisha: What about concurrency? If we have 150 concurrent users typing small queries, will batching kick in and hurt latency?
02:28 Diego: Our runtime does continuous batching — for small requests, batching can improve throughput and reduce cost, but we have latency SLO knobs. For hosted mode we default to a latency-first policy for tiered accounts. If your workload is very latency-sensitive at 95th pct, Dedicated lets you pin GPU pools and reduce cross-tenant batching.
02:50 Tom: Can you show how retries look? We have transient network blips and occasional 502s from upstreams.
02:55 Diego: Yep. We recommend idempotency keys + client-side exponential backoff with jitter. Example: send a request with idempotency_key: uuid4(). On retry, the server returns a 409 or dedup token or the same response object so you don't double-apply. I'll share a node/python snippet in the repo.
03:18 Diego: (reads snippet) backoff = min(base * 2**attempt, max); jitter=random(); sleep(base + jitter). For streaming: we recommend reconnecting with a resume token where possible — if not available, re-run with the same idempotency key and the runtime will serve cached prefix if we have KV cache for recent tokens.
03:40 Samir: How long is the KV cache retained? Anything stored that might include PII?
03:45 Priya (Redwood Product): KV cache retention is configurable per-customer; by default short-lived (a few minutes) and you can disable prefix caching entirely. For PII we suggest redaction before sending, or use Private deployment with customer-managed KMS if you need tenant isolation. We'll send our doc on retention + encryption.
04:10 Maya: Quick demo of a failure scenario. (diego triggers simulated upstream 502) You'll see stream cut and a client reconnect attempt with the same idempotency key. The console trace shows the fallback to reissue vs resume.
04:38 Diego: Notice the trace: route -> model variant fallback (rdx-lite-3b-fp16) then a short retry. This is how graceful degradation keeps UX alive while preserving cost.
04:55 Nora: If the model falls back, is the output quality flagged or is there any alert?
05:01 Priya: We surface model-variant fallback in the Console with an event flag and you can set an alert to notify on >X% fallback rate. Also we log model variant used per-request for post-hoc QA.
05:17 Aisha: How do we handle duplicates on retries for create-ticket flows? We need idempotent writes to our ticket system.
05:23 Diego: Put the idempotency key into your ticket microservice call as well — when you re-run the generation request with same key, check if response already produced a ticket id and return it. On Redwood side, the request metadata includes your key so we won't generate duplicate outputs for the same key if the pipeline completed. We'll share the pattern example.
05:40 Tom: Any built-in support for at-most-once semantics?
05:44 Diego: At-most-once across the whole pipeline is hard; typical pattern is idempotent consumer side. For ack-level semantics we recommend storing a mapping of idempotency key -> result and use an intermediate dedupe store (redis).
06:05 Nora: You mentioned Optimize — can you show recommendations for our use case? We're a lot of short queries.
06:12 Priya: Sure. (screen) Optimize analyzes sample traces and suggests: 1) use per-route smaller batch sizes, 2) enable prefix KV cache for repeated prompts, 3) quantized model candidates for cheaper inference. For support chat we often recommend 8-bit quantized medium models to trade a bit of quality for 5–7x cost savings.
06:35 Aisha: Any metrics we get out of the box to validate regressions if we switch quantized models?
06:40 Priya: Yes — per-route quality metrics and sample-based evals; you can upload a prompt set and the console runs A/B quality checks and flags regressed prompts with diffs.
06:52 Tom: For production telemetry, can we export traces to our datadog?
06:56 Diego: Absolutely — we have tracing hooks and can forward request traces and token-level metrics to Datadog or your SIEM. We'll include the trace schema in the repo.
07:08 Samir: About keys: do you support customer-managed KMS for hosted?
07:11 Priya: Hosted supports envelope encryption and customer-managed KMS via cloud-KMS integration for Enterprise plans. For strict regulatory needs we offer Private deployment in your VPC with HSM options.
07:25 Aisha: What's the expected tail latency for streamed responses at 50 qps with 1k token short outputs?
07:32 Diego: Rough ballpark on hosted: 95th pct ~180–350ms for small responses on optimized routes; depends heavily on model and batching. Dedicated with pinned GPU pools can cut the 95th down to ~80–120ms in many cases; we'll need to benchmark with your exact prompt mix.
07:52 Maya: We'll include a bench workbook — fill in your QPS, avg tokens, and desired percentile and we'll return a recommended config (model, batching, dedicated vs hosted).
08:06 Nora: Can you show retry headers in the response? We want to audit when retries occurred.
08:11 Diego: Yes — the response metadata includes attempt_count, retry_reason, and model_variant. The Console also shows a timeline for each request with retry events.
08:25 Aisha: One more — how do web-socket connections behave under network oscillation? Does the SDK reconnect gracefully?
08:30 Diego: Our SDK does automatic reconnection + resume if resume tokens are enabled; otherwise we reissue request with the same idempotency key for dedupe. We'll send example code for the JS SDK that shows the reconnect + partial-merge logic.
08:48 Tom: Any rate limit patterns? We're worried about 429 storms during a traffic spike.
08:53 Maya: We expose per-route quotas and client-side recommended leaky-bucket token rate. On the backend we do graceful throttling and prioritized routing for paid tiers. We'll share our recommended client backoff config and leaky-bucket parameters.
09:05 Nora: Great — can we get a short POC proposal after this?
09:08 Maya: Yes. High-level pilot: one-week bench (we run load tests), two-week functional trial with a 100-user beta, and observability handoff. Diego will scope the bench.
09:18 Diego: I'll need your traffic sample and a couple representative prompts. Also any redaction rules for PII.
09:24 Aisha: We'll send that by Monday.
09:28 Maya: Quick recap of next steps: security docs, idempotency code, bench workbook, and schedule pilot scoping. Anything else?
09:36 Samir: Please include retention and deletion policy detail in the security doc.
09:40 Maya: Noted. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
---
End of transcript
